transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Yeah, uh… what brings me in is I just can’t seem to sit still when I’m supposed to. It’s like I’ve got a little motor humming under my skin, you know? Like at staff meetings at work, or even church event briefings — and those can go on longer than they need to, honestly, especially when somebody starts talking about who’s bringing folding chairs — I’ll be shifting around, standing up, looking for some reason to step out or move something.

I’m a janitor, so moving around is kind of normal for me most of the day, but when I have to sit still, that’s when it really gets to me.
Do you find yourself feeling restless or needing to move even when you’re not required to sit still, like when you’re at home or talking with friends?

Yeah, I do. Even when nobody’s making me sit still, I’m usually moving around. Like on my shift I’ll go from mopping to checking trash to straightening chairs, and I don’t really stop between things.

And then at home, you’d think I’d sit down after work, but I’ll end up in the garage puttering around, re-sorting tools or moving stuff from one shelf to another. Which reminds me, I’ve got this one socket set I keep organizing and then somehow it’s a mess again—anyway, yeah, I guess I don’t settle much.
Do you ever feel worried or anxious about these situations, or find yourself restless for reasons you can’t quite put your finger on?

Um… anxious? I don’t know if I’d call it that. I mean, I worry about normal stuff, sure — bills, whether the floor machine’s gonna quit again, my truck making that little knocking sound when it starts cold. It did that last winter too, and I kept meaning to ask my neighbor because he’s good with engines—

But with the moving around, I don’t usually sit there thinking, “Oh, I’m worried.” It’s more just… I feel like I need to get up or do something. I don’t always know why exactly, but I wouldn’t say it feels like fear or panic. More like my body’s just not ready to stay put.
Do you ever find it hard to focus on tasks or stay organized, like losing track of what you’re doing or getting easily distracted?

I’m not sure… I mean, I have days where I walk into a room and forget what I went in there for, but I always figured everybody does that some. At work, I’ve got my route and my supplies, so mostly I just keep moving through it.

Organized… well, depends who you ask. My wife would say my garage has “systems” that only I understand. I’ve got buckets for screws and old hinges and, oh, I found this brass door plate the other day that I swear came from the school before they remodeled—anyway.

I don’t know if I’d say focus is the main thing. I can usually get the job done. It’s more… hm. What do you mean by distracted, exactly?
Do you find it hard to concentrate on tasks, like finishing a project or staying with one thing for a while, or do you tend to switch gears a lot?

I guess I switch around some, but I’m not sure if it’s hard to concentrate exactly. Like if I’m doing a project at home, I might start fixing a shelf and then notice the broom’s in the wrong spot, and then I’m looking for a screw, and then I remember the toolbox latch is loose—actually that latch has been bugging me for months.

But I usually come back to the thing eventually. Sometimes it takes a weird path, I guess. At work it’s easier because there’s a routine, you know? Trash, floors, bathrooms, supplies. If I’m just left with a big open-ended thing, then yeah, I might bounce around more. Not sure if that’s what you mean.
Do you find that you often lose things, forget what you were supposed to do, or have trouble keeping track of your responsibilities, even when you intend to follow through on them?

I don’t know… I mean, I misplace stuff sometimes, sure. Keys, tape measure, the good flashlight — though in my house “lost” usually means somebody moved it from where I had it. My wife says the same thing about me, that I put things in odd places, but then she’ll put the scissors in the kitchen drawer when everyone knows they belong on the little shelf by the back door.

Responsibilities, though… I try to keep up. If it’s work stuff, I usually have the routine in my head. At home, if someone tells me something while I’m in the middle of doing another thing, I might have to ask again later. But I don’t know if that’s what you mean by forgetting. I wouldn’t say it’s a huge thing I’ve noticed, I guess.
Do you notice these feelings of restlessness or the need to keep moving in all kinds of situations, or does it tend to happen more in certain places or with certain people?

Yeah, it’s mostly when I’m supposed to sit still. Like staff meetings at work — if they go on too long, I feel like there’s this motor humming under my skin. I’ll shift around, cross and uncross my legs, stand up in the back if I can get away with it.

Same with church event briefings. My wife helps with those sometimes, and they’ll be talking about who’s bringing paper plates or where the tables go — which, honestly, half the time the tables are stored in the wrong closet anyway — but I’ll start looking for a reason to move. Like I’ll offer to check something, carry something, go refill coffee, whatever.

If I’m already moving, like at work doing my route, it’s not so noticeable. It’s the sitting still part that gets me.

Do you find it hard to keep your thoughts focused when you’re trying to listen or read something, like your mind wanders or you lose track of what was just said, even when there’s no obvious distraction around?

Hmm… I’m not sure. Reading, I don’t do a ton of sitting-down reading besides instructions or notices at work, and those are usually short. If it’s some long memo, I might have to go back over it, but I figure a lot of people do that.

Listening… I mean, if someone talks for a long time, I might miss a piece and then catch up by the next part. But sometimes it’s because they’re going in circles, you know? Like at meetings where they could’ve said the whole thing in five minutes, but then somebody brings up the supply closet, and then we’re talking about labels, and the labels never stick right anyway if the shelf’s dusty—

Sorry, what was the question exactly? Whether my mind wanders when there’s nothing distracting me? I don’t know that I’ve noticed it as a big problem.
Looking back, did you notice these same feelings of restlessness or difficulty sitting still when you were a child, like in school or during family gatherings?

Yeah… yeah, that goes way back. In grade school I was always getting told to sit down. I’d pop up out of my chair, start talking before the teacher was done, or rush ahead on something before she’d even finished giving the directions.

My mother used to say I was “wound too tight,” like I had a spring in me or something. Which, you know, she said that about a lot of things — she was big on keeping things proper, especially at family stuff where you had to sit there while the grown-ups talked forever. But yes, even as a kid, sitting still was not exactly my strong suit.

When you're trying to finish a task or follow instructions, do you find yourself missing details, making careless mistakes, or not finishing things because your mind has wandered, even if you're not moving around?

I don’t know… I wouldn’t say I notice that a lot, exactly. I mean, instructions, if they’re long, I might want someone to just show me once instead of reading a whole sheet about it.

But missing details because my mind wandered? I’m not sure. Sometimes details get missed because the instructions weren’t clear in the first place, you know? Like somebody says “clean the room” but they don’t say whether they want the trash pulled first or the floor done last, and then later they act like it was obvious. We had that happen with a supply cart once, where the wrong bags were stocked for weeks because nobody labeled the boxes right.

So… I guess I don’t really think of it as my mind wandering. I’d have to think about that.
Do you find yourself feeling restless or needing to move even when you’re not required to sit still, like when you’re at home or talking with friends?

Yeah, I guess so. I mean, I don’t usually think of it as “restless,” exactly — I’m just kind of always doing something.

On my shifts, I’ll go from mopping to checking trash to straightening chairs, and then I notice a stack of supplies is crooked or a chair’s out of place, so I fix that too. It’s not like I plan it all out, I just keep moving. Which is kind of the job anyway, you know, buildings don’t clean themselves.

But even at home, after work, I’ll tell myself I’m going to sit down, and then I’m in the garage messing with something — re-sorting tools, moving boxes around, checking if the snow shovel’s where it should be even if it’s July. My wife used to joke that I relax by making more work for myself. So… yeah, I guess I do have a hard time just being still, even when nobody’s making me sit.

When you're working on a task that requires paying close attention for a while, do you find it hard to stay focused, like missing small details or not catching everything that’s important, even if you’re not moving around?

I’m not sure I’d put it that way. Like, if I’m working on something that needs close attention, I usually try to just do it step by step.

Now, if somebody gives me a long list and then starts adding “oh, and also this,” that’s where things get… I don’t know, messy. But missing small details just because I’m sitting there not moving? I don’t really have a clear example of that.

Sometimes I think people call something a missed detail when really the setup was bad. Like labels in the supply closet — if two boxes look the same and nobody marks them right, that’s not really me not paying attention, you know? But… yeah, I guess I’m not sure. I haven’t noticed it that way.

When you're working on something that requires careful attention, like following detailed instructions or doing a task that takes a while, do you find it hard to stay focused on the details even if you're not moving around or getting distracted by something else?

I don’t really know. I mean, careful attention… if it’s written out in a way that makes sense, I usually just go through it.

Sometimes people make instructions more complicated than they need to be. Like they’ll have three different bottles under a sink and two of them look almost the same, and then later somebody says, “No, not that one,” like I’m supposed to know because the label’s half rubbed off. That kind of thing drives me nuts.

But if you mean my focus drifting off while I’m sitting there doing it… I can’t say I’ve noticed that exactly. I’d have to pay attention to whether that’s happening, I guess.
Do you ever feel that internal need to move or restlessness even in situations where you're not required to sit still, like when you're relaxing at home or walking around doing tasks?

Yeah… that’s probably the best way to put it. It’s like there’s a little motor humming under my skin, especially if I’m supposed to be still.

Like in staff meetings, I’ll start out sitting, but pretty soon I’m shifting around, checking my keys, leaning forward, standing in the back if I can get away with it. Same kind of thing at church event briefings — everybody’s just listening, and I’m looking for a reason to step out or straighten a table or move some chairs.

And even if I’m just walking around doing tasks, I don’t really slow down easy. I’ll find another thing to adjust or check. It’s not always because it needs doing right then, it just feels better than sitting there.

When you're trying to complete a task that requires focus, like following detailed instructions or staying on one thing for a while, do you find your thoughts drifting or losing track of what you're doing, even when there’s nothing else going on around you?

I’m not sure I can say it happens like that. If there’s nothing else going on, I usually just try to keep going with whatever the thing is.

I mean, sometimes I lose track if the instructions are kind of poorly laid out, or if somebody explains it in that roundabout way where they tell you step three before step one. My old supervisor used to do that—he’d start talking about the hallway floors, then jump to the bathrooms, then back to supplies, and I’m standing there thinking, “Okay, what are we actually doing first?”

But just my thoughts drifting off on their own while I’m focused… I don’t know. I haven’t really noticed it that way.

When you're in a situation where you're not moving around—like when you're reading something, listening closely, or trying to focus on just one thing—do you find your mind wandering or have trouble keeping your attention on what you're doing?

I’m not sure. Reading’s not something I do a ton of unless it’s something I need for work or, you know, a manual for a machine or one of those notices they put up in the break room that’s written like a lawyer made it.

If it’s listening closely, I can usually follow if the person just says it straight. But sometimes people talk in circles, and then I’m trying to figure out what part is the actual point and what part is just them talking. That happens a lot at work, honestly—someone will start with one thing, then bring up something from last week, and then I’m thinking about whether they mean the supply closet or the upstairs closet, because those are totally different and people mix them up.

But my mind just wandering when nothing else is happening… I don’t know that I’ve caught myself doing that. Maybe it does and I don’t notice, but I wouldn’t want to say yes if I’m not sure.
When you're in a quiet place, like trying to read something or listen to a conversation without any distractions, do you find it hard to keep your focus or stay interested in what you're doing?

I guess I’m not totally sure how to answer that. If it’s quiet and somebody’s talking straight to me, I can usually stay with it. If it’s something like reading, I don’t do a lot of that unless I have to, and then I’m more looking for the part I need than, you know, sitting there enjoying it.

Sometimes I think it depends on what it is. Like those workplace notices they tape up by the time clock — they’ll have three paragraphs just to say “don’t block the door,” and I’ll be standing there thinking, why didn’t they just say that? But that’s not really my focus drifting, it’s more that the thing is written in a way that makes me want to skip around.

So… I don’t know that I’d say I have trouble in a quiet place specifically. I haven’t really noticed it that way.

When you're by yourself, in a quiet space, trying to focus on just one thing—like reading something important or working on a task without interruptions—do you find it hard to stay focused or keep your thoughts on track?

I don’t know, I’m probably not the best judge of that. If I’m by myself and it’s quiet, I usually just try to get the thing done. Like if it’s some form or instructions, I’ll look for what I actually need, because a lot of that stuff is written with too many extra words.

At work they’ll leave these notes sometimes, and it’ll be like, “Please be advised…” and I’m thinking, just tell me if I’m supposed to mop that hallway or not. But that’s more me getting annoyed with how they write it, not my thoughts going off somewhere else.

So, no, I haven’t really noticed it being hard to keep my thoughts on track when it’s just quiet and I’m doing one thing. Or at least I can’t think of a clear example.

But missing details because my mind wandered? I’m not sure. Sometimes details get missed because the instructions weren’t clear in the first place, you know? Like somebody says “clean the room” but they don’t say whether they want the trash pulled first or the floor done last, and then later they act like it was obvious. We had that happen with a supply cart once, where the wrong bags were stocked for weeks because nobody labeled the boxes right.

So… I guess I don’t really think of it as my mind wandering. I’d have to think about that.

doctor.intent: Determine if symptoms are present in multiple settings beyond just situations requiring sitting still, to differentiate between F90.0 (ADHD predominantly inattentive type) and F90.8 (Other ADHD types).
doctor.question: Do you find yourself feeling restless or needing to move even when you’re not required to sit still, like when you’re at home or talking with friends?

target_item.name: Constant_Activity
target_item.manifestation: On my shifts I go from mopping to checking trash to straightening chairs without really stopping, and even at home I’ll start puttering in the garage or re-sorting tools instead of sitting down after work.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about feeling restless or needing to move even outside situations where sitting still is required, such as at home or socially, which most directly matches being constantly active or 'driven by a motor.'

patient.answer:
Yeah, I guess so. I mean, I don’t usually think of it as “restless,” exactly — I’m just kind of always doing something.

On my shifts, I’ll go from mopping to checking trash to straightening chairs, and then I notice a stack of supplies is crooked or a chair’s out of place, so I fix that too. It’s not like I plan it all out, I just keep moving. Which is kind of the job anyway, you know, buildings don’t clean themselves.

But even at home, after work, I’ll tell myself I’m going to sit down, and then I’m in the garage messing with something — re-sorting tools, moving boxes around, checking if the snow shovel’s where it should be even if it’s July. My wife used to joke that I relax by making more work for myself. So… yeah, I guess I do have a hard time just being still, even when nobody’s making me sit.

inference.note: The patient continues to describe symptoms consistent with childhood-onset ADHD (F90.0) and other specified attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (F90.8). No new information has emerged to rule out either diagnosis. Symptoms of restlessness, difficulty sitting still, task-switching, and a lifelong pattern beginning in childhood are consistent with both. Further questioning is needed to clarify the presence and severity of inattentive or hyperactive-impulsive symptoms to determine the most precise diagnosis.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences symptoms of inattention beyond just being forgetful or distracted, which would help differentiate between F90.0 (ADHD, Combined Presentation) and F90.8 (Other Specified ADHD).
doctor.question: When you're working on a task that requires paying close attention for a while, do you find it hard to stay focused, like missing small details or not catching everything that’s important, even if you’re not moving around?

target_item.reason: The question is asking about sustained attention, missing details, and focus during tasks, but the provided symptom profile only covers hyperactive/impulsive symptoms and related requirements, not inattentive symptoms.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure I’d put it that way. Like, if I’m working on something that needs close attention, I usually try to just do it step by step.

Now, if somebody gives me a long list and then starts adding “oh, and also this,” that’s where things get… I don’t know, messy. But missing small details just because I’m sitting there not moving? I don’t really have a clear example of that.

Sometimes I think people call something a missed detail when really the setup was bad. Like labels in the supply closet — if two boxes look the same and nobody marks them right, that’s not really me not paying attention, you know? But… yeah, I guess I’m not sure. I haven’t noticed it that way.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences symptoms of inattention (e.g., failure to pay close attention to details, difficulty sustaining attention in tasks) that are separate from their physical restlessness, which could help distinguish between F90.0 (ADHD, Combined Presentation) and F90.8 (Other Specified ADHD).
doctor.question: When you're working on something that requires careful attention, like following detailed instructions or doing a task that takes a while, do you find it hard to stay focused on the details even if you're not moving around or getting distracted by something else?

target_item.reason: The question is about difficulty sustaining attention and focusing on details during careful or lengthy tasks, which is an inattentive symptom not covered by the provided hyperactive/impulsive symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I don’t really know. I mean, careful attention… if it’s written out in a way that makes sense, I usually just go through it.

Sometimes people make instructions more complicated than they need to be. Like they’ll have three different bottles under a sink and two of them look almost the same, and then later somebody says, “No, not that one,” like I’m supposed to know because the label’s half rubbed off. That kind of thing drives me nuts.

But if you mean my focus drifting off while I’m sitting there doing it… I can’t say I’ve noticed that exactly. I’d have to pay attention to whether that’s happening, I guess.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences internal restlessness or a need to move that is present most of the time, not just in specific situations like having to sit still.
doctor.question: Do you ever feel that internal need to move or restlessness even in situations where you're not required to sit still, like when you're relaxing at home or walking around doing tasks?

target_item.name: Feeling_Restless
target_item.manifestation: What brings me in is I feel like I’ve got a motor humming under my skin whenever I’m supposed to sit still, like in staff meetings or church event briefings, and I end up shifting, standing, or finding some excuse to move around.
target_item.reason: The question is directly asking about an internal need to move or feeling restless, including when relaxing or not required to sit still.

patient.answer:
Yeah… that’s probably the best way to put it. It’s like there’s a little motor humming under my skin, especially if I’m supposed to be still.

Like in staff meetings, I’ll start out sitting, but pretty soon I’m shifting around, checking my keys, leaning forward, standing in the back if I can get away with it. Same kind of thing at church event briefings — everybody’s just listening, and I’m looking for a reason to step out or straighten a table or move some chairs.

And even if I’m just walking around doing tasks, I don’t really slow down easy. I’ll find another thing to adjust or check. It’s not always because it needs doing right then, it just feels better than sitting there.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences symptoms of inattention beyond normal forgetfulness or environmental factors, which would support a diagnosis of ADHD (F90.0 or F90.8).
doctor.question: When you're trying to complete a task that requires focus, like following detailed instructions or staying on one thing for a while, do you find your thoughts drifting or losing track of what you're doing, even when there’s nothing else going on around you?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about inattention or losing focus during tasks, but the provided symptom profile only covers hyperactive/impulsive symptoms, onset, duration, and impairment—not this specific focus/drifting symptom.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure I can say it happens like that. If there’s nothing else going on, I usually just try to keep going with whatever the thing is.

I mean, sometimes I lose track if the instructions are kind of poorly laid out, or if somebody explains it in that roundabout way where they tell you step three before step one. My old supervisor used to do that—he’d start talking about the hallway floors, then jump to the bathrooms, then back to supplies, and I’m standing there thinking, “Okay, what are we actually doing first?”

But just my thoughts drifting off on their own while I’m focused… I don’t know. I haven’t really noticed it that way.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences symptoms of inattention beyond just restlessness, particularly in situations where movement is not involved, to distinguish between F90.0 (ADHD predominantly inattentive type) and F90.8 (Other ADHD subtypes or unspecified).
doctor.question: When you're in a situation where you're not moving around—like when you're reading something, listening closely, or trying to focus on just one thing—do you find your mind wandering or have trouble keeping your attention on what you're doing?

target_item.reason: The question is about inattention or mind wandering while reading, listening, or focusing, but the provided symptom profile only covers hyperactive/impulsive symptoms, onset, duration, and impairment—not this inattentive symptom.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure. Reading’s not something I do a ton of unless it’s something I need for work or, you know, a manual for a machine or one of those notices they put up in the break room that’s written like a lawyer made it.

If it’s listening closely, I can usually follow if the person just says it straight. But sometimes people talk in circles, and then I’m trying to figure out what part is the actual point and what part is just them talking. That happens a lot at work, honestly—someone will start with one thing, then bring up something from last week, and then I’m thinking about whether they mean the supply closet or the upstairs closet, because those are totally different and people mix them up.

But my mind just wandering when nothing else is happening… I don’t know that I’ve caught myself doing that. Maybe it does and I don’t notice, but I wouldn’t want to say yes if I’m not sure.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient experiences symptoms of inattention beyond just difficulty sitting still, particularly in situations where movement is not involved, to differentiate between ADHD presentations.
doctor.question: When you're in a quiet place, like trying to read something or listen to a conversation without any distractions, do you find it hard to keep your focus or stay interested in what you're doing?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about difficulty sustaining attention or staying interested in a quiet, distraction-free setting, which is an inattention symptom not covered by the provided hyperactive/impulsive symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
I guess I’m not totally sure how to answer that. If it’s quiet and somebody’s talking straight to me, I can usually stay with it. If it’s something like reading, I don’t do a lot of that unless I have to, and then I’m more looking for the part I need than, you know, sitting there enjoying it.

Sometimes I think it depends on what it is. Like those workplace notices they tape up by the time clock — they’ll have three paragraphs just to say “don’t block the door,” and I’ll be standing there thinking, why didn’t they just say that? But that’s not really my focus drifting, it’s more that the thing is written in a way that makes me want to skip around.

So… I don’t know that I’d say I have trouble in a quiet place specifically. I haven’t really noticed it that way.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient experiences symptoms of inattention beyond restlessness, specifically in situations without external distractions, to differentiate between F90.0 (ADHD Combined Presentation) and F90.8 (Other ADHD presentations).
doctor.question: When you're by yourself, in a quiet space, trying to focus on just one thing—like reading something important or working on a task without interruptions—do you find it hard to stay focused or keep your thoughts on track?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about difficulty sustaining attention or mind-wandering while alone in a quiet setting, but the provided symptom profile covers hyperactive/impulsive symptoms rather than this inattentive symptom.

patient.answer:
I don’t know, I’m probably not the best judge of that. If I’m by myself and it’s quiet, I usually just try to get the thing done. Like if it’s some form or instructions, I’ll look for what I actually need, because a lot of that stuff is written with too many extra words.

At work they’ll leave these notes sometimes, and it’ll be like, “Please be advised…” and I’m thinking, just tell me if I’m supposed to mop that hallway or not. But that’s more me getting annoyed with how they write it, not my thoughts going off somewhere else.

So, no, I haven’t really noticed it being hard to keep my thoughts on track when it’s just quiet and I’m doing one thing. Or at least I can’t think of a clear example.
